video.title: Why Was Jesus ASLEEP in the Storm? The Old Testament Story Mark Is Retelling
video.description:
Why was Jesus asleep in the boat while the storm raged on the Sea of Galilee, and why does Mark make such a point of showing it? The answer is hidden in another storm every Jewish listener already knew by heart, and once you hear it, the story of Jesus calming the storm will never read the same way again.

In this Bible study we walk slowly through Mark 4:35 to 41 in the King James Version and set it beside Jonah chapter 1, verse by verse. You will see how both stories share a great wind, a ship about to break apart, one man asleep while everyone else fights for their lives, and a terrified crew waking him with almost the same words: "that we perish not" and "carest thou not that we perish?" We look at the Hebrew word for Jonah's heavy sleep, radam, and how the Septuagint renders it with the very verb Mark uses for Jesus, katheudo. We trace the word "great" through Jonah's chapter and discover that Mark's closing line, "they feared exceedingly," literally reads "they feared a great fear," using the same three Greek words found in the Greek text of Jonah 1:10. Then we reach the moment the two stories split apart: Jonah's sea grows calm only when a man is thrown into it, but Jesus simply stands up and commands the wind with the same word he used to silence a demon in the synagogue at Capernaum. Through Psalm 89, Psalm 65, Job 38, and Psalm 107, you will see why the disciples' fear shifted from the water to the man in their boat. We also explore why the Psalms speak both of a God who never sleeps and of a God the faithful begged to wake up, the meaning of the single word for "pillow" that appears only in Mark, the ancient fishing boat uncovered on the shore of Galilee in 1986, and the link between "the Son of man hath not where to lay his head" and the cross. Finally, we consider the tradition that Mark's Gospel preserves Peter's own memories, and what the letter that bears Peter's name says about the question "Do you not care?"

Which detail surprised you most? Share your thoughts in the comments, and subscribe so you do not miss the next study as we keep opening the Scriptures together.

Sources mentioned:
King James Version
The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures)
Papias
Eusebius
The Ginosar boat (Sea of Galilee boat, discovered 1986)

transcript.text: Evening has come on the Sea of Galilee.
A wind rises.
The waves beat into the boat, and the boat is filling with water.
At the back, one man is lying with his head on a cushion.
He is asleep.
You know this story.
But here is the question almost nobody stops to ask.
Why is Jesus asleep?
Not how could he sleep.
Why does Mark want you to see him sleeping?
Because Mark is not only reporting a storm, he is telling it in a way that sounds like another storm.
One every Jewish listener already knew by heart.
A ship in danger, terrified sailors, and one man asleep below while everyone else fights for their lives.
That is the story of Jonah.
Mark even gives you a small detail no other gospel writer keeps.
He says Jesus was asleep on a pillow.
In Greek, it is proskephalaion, "a cushion for the head."
It is the only time that word appears in the whole New Testament.
Remember that cushion, we will come back to it.
But if Mark is echoing Jonah, the comparison seems to run the wrong way.
Jonah was asleep because he was running from God.
He was the reason the storm came at all.
So why would Mark place Jesus of all people in the exact position of a runaway prophet?
Let us look at what Mark actually wrote.
Mark 4:35 to 41 in the King James version.
And the same day, when the even was come, he saith unto them, Let us pass over unto the other side.
Verse 37.
And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full.
Verse 38.
And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow, and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?
Notice what Mark does in that verse.
He does not say the disciples asked Jesus for help.
He says they woke him.
And what comes out of their mouths is not a prayer, it is an accusation.
Carest thou not?
Do you not care?
These are fishermen.
Several of them have worked this lake their whole lives.
They know when a boat is lost, and the one person who could do something is lying on a cushion.
Now step onto a different ship.
It is sailing west from the port of Joppa out into the open Mediterranean.
A man has paid his fare and gone down into it.
His name is Jonah.
God has told him to go east to Nineveh.
He is going as far west as a ship will take him.
Jonah chapter 1, verse 4.
But the Lord sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken.
Verse 5.
Then the mariners were afraid and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea to lighten it of them.
But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship, and he lay and was fast asleep.
Fast asleep.
While the sailors throw their cargo overboard.
Verse 6.
So the shipmaster came to him and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper?
Arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us that we perish not.
Put the two scenes side by side.
A great wind on the water, a boat about to break apart, one man asleep in the lowest or farthest part of the vessel.

transcript.text: God sends a great wind in verse 4.
There is a great tempest in the same verse.
The King James calls it mighty.
Jonah calls it this great tempest in verse 12.
And in verse 17, a great fish.
The whole chapter is built on that one adjective.
Go back to Mark.
There arose a great storm of wind.
Verse 39, after Jesus speaks, there was a great calm.
And then verse 41, and they feared exceedingly.
That last phrase in English hides something.
In Greek, Mark writes ephobethesan phobon megan.
Word for word, they feared a great fear.
Now open Jonah chapter 1, verse 10.
Then were the men exceedingly afraid.
The Hebrew says, Vayiru ha'anashim yira gedola.
The men feared a great fear.
And the Greek translation of that verse uses the same three words Mark wrote, ephobethesan phobon megan, with only the men standing between them.
Sit with that.
A great storm, a great calm, a great fear.
Three times Mark reaches for the word great, and the last time he reaches into Jonah's own sentence to do it.
A great many New Testament scholars recognize this as a deliberate echo.
For a listener who grew up hearing Jonah read aloud, that closing line would have rung like a bell.
Now go back to the moment the two stories split apart.
Because they do split, and the place where they part is where Mark's real point lives.
Jonah's sailors try everything.
They throw the cargo overboard, they pray to every God they know.
Finally, they ask Jonah what to do.
Jonah chapter 1, verse 12.
Take me up and cast me forth into the sea.
So shall the sea be calm unto you.
For I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you.
They do not want to.
They row harder.
It does not work.
Verse 15.
So they took up Jonah and cast him forth into the sea, and the sea ceased from her raging.
In Jonah, the sea becomes calm only when a man is thrown into it.
Now watch Jesus.
Mark 4:39.
And he arose and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still.
And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
No one is thrown overboard.
Jesus stands up and speaks.
Two words in Greek.
The first is siopa, which means be silent.
And pephimoso, which literally means be muzzled.
It is what you say to an animal that will not stop growling.
And Mark has used that verb before.
In chapter 1, in the synagogue at Capernaum, a man with an unclean spirit cries out.
Mark 1:25.
And Jesus rebuked him saying, Hold thy peace and come out of him.
Hold thy peace is the same verb, be muzzled.
And the word rebuked is the same as well, epitimao.
Jesus speaks to the wind and the waves on the lake the same way he spoke to a demon in a synagogue.
He does not plead with the sea.
He gives it an order.
Now ask what a first-century Jew would have made of that.
In the Hebrew scriptures, who commands the sea?
Psalm 89:9.
Thou rulest the raging of the sea, when the waves thereof arise, thou stillest them.
That is spoken to the Lord.
Psalm 65:7.
